title: codex-site-kit rule
description: One rule in the rulebook. Every field except the optional ones is load-bearing: a finding printed to a beginner must be able to answer WHAT it is, WHY it matters, WHO says so with what strength of evidence, and WHAT TO DO. A rule that cannot fill those four is not shippable.

id.description: Stable identifier. Never reused, never renumbered. A finding in a report from six months ago must still resolve.

tier.description: 1/2/3 are the corpus's own tiers, ranked by how fast a non-technical owner clocks the tell on a phone. `floor` is the mobile/performance floor: not aesthetics, the failures that make a page look broken. `craft` is quality that raises competence without being a tell. `honesty` is truthfulness of claims. `trap` currently reads as sophisticated and will not. `ledger` is cross-build.

category.description: What part of the craft this belongs to. Used to group a report.

title.description: The name of the move, the way a chess book names an opening. Short enough to scan in a list.

what_it_is.description: The observable thing, described so someone could point at it on a screen. No judgement in this field.

why_it_matters.description: The consequence. Preferably the mechanism, not the adjective: what actually goes wrong, for whom, on what device.

name.description: A key in sources.json. Validation fails otherwise.

where.description: The section, gate number or rule name inside that source.

quote.description: The source's own words, where they are the clearest statement of the rule.

also_in.description: Independent corroboration. Two tools agreeing by copying each other is not corroboration; this field is only for sources that arrived at the rule separately.

confidence_note.description: REQUIRED whenever source.confidence is ASSERTED or INFERRED. States plainly what is not proven, so the tool can print it and the reader can discount it. This is how a hypothesis is stopped from hardening into a gate.

detector.description: How to test it. `kind` selects an evaluator in engine.js; the remaining properties are that evaluator's parameters. Two kinds never run automatically and say so: `browser` needs a live render, `manual` needs a human or a vision model.

threshold.description: The exact trigger, written so a person can check the tool's arithmetic. 'Puffy' is not a threshold. '>= 3 blurred non-inset layers, OR >= 2 where any alpha > 0.12, OR 1 blurred layer with alpha > 0.30' is.

threshold_provenance.description: Where the NUMBER came from, which is often not where the RULE came from. `from_source`: the cited source published this number. `calibrated_here`: the source named the tell without a number and the number was fitted against the preview corpus. `arithmetic`: defensible reasoning, nobody published it. The corpus's own `--stagger: 45ms` is the cautionary case.

severity.description: `fail` = the corpus treats it as a hard gate. `warn` = real but contestable, or context-dependent. `info` = worth knowing, never blocking. An ASSERTED rule may not be `fail` unless the corpus itself gates on it.

fix.description: The better move. Concrete enough to apply without a second search: the replacement value, the deletion, or the named alternative.

fix_code.description: The literal replacement, where one exists and is short.

teach.description: Two or three sentences for a complete beginner. Every technical word either avoided or defined in place. This is the field that makes the linter a curriculum rather than a scoreboard.

chess.description: Optional. A chess analogy, only where it genuinely clarifies the idea rather than decorating it. Used sparingly and deliberately.

burned_on.description: Trap tier only. The date the corpus recorded this signal as already burned — read as slop rather than as sophistication.

review_by.description: The date after which this rule must be re-validated against fresh evidence or retired. Past it, engine.js downgrades the rule to `info` and prints that nobody has re-checked it. Rules about taste rot; rules about arithmetic do not. Only the ones that rot carry this.

decay.description: What is happening to this tell over time. febbhav is the only source in the corpus tracking decay, which is why most rules leave this empty rather than guessing.

applies_to.description: Delivery contexts this rule governs. A rule written for a one-file page AirDropped to a phone does not automatically govern a hosted multi-file site, and the corpus supersedes three of its own rules on exactly that boundary.

supersedes.description: Rule ids this one replaces in a given delivery context.

measured.description: What this detector actually found when run over the preview corpus on 2026-09-17. Present only where it was run. A rulebook that claims to catch slop and finds none in a corpus already proven slop-ridden is wrong, and this field is where that gets checked.

suppress_when.description: A project-context flag under which this rule does not apply. A rule that fires on the right thing in the wrong context is still a wrong finding: publishing LocalBusiness structured data is the cheapest win on a real site and precisely what the mitigation set forbids on an unsolicited concept page. The engine skips the rule and says why.
